title: Modern JavaScript Concepts
body:
Interview prep note. See [[JavaScript]] and [[DOM]] for the course-notes versions.

## Core Facts to Know

- [[HTML]] is the script describing what the page should be; the [[DOM]] is that script built out into live objects.
- The DOM is a tree of node objects the browser maintains in memory, on your machine.
- The DOM is queried and mutated with `document.querySelector`, `element.textContent`, and friends.
- [[Reflow]] is layout recalculation and is expensive.
- [[Repaint]] only redraws pixels and is cheaper than reflow.
- Both reflow and repaint happen on your machine, triggered by the rendering engine after a DOM mutation.
- The [[Virtual DOM]] is a lightweight JS object tree, not a browser feature.
- The virtual DOM is diffed against the previous version entirely in the JS engine, before any real DOM is touched.
- [[Reconciliation]] is working out the minimum set of real DOM changes needed.
- Framework code runs in the same renderer process as your own code.
- The [[Call Stack]] shows which function called which.
- Breakpoints pause the JS engine's execution.
- The DevTools Network tab records requests on your machine, but shows activity that also touched the network and their machine.
- [[Source Maps]] map shipped minified code back to original source files.
- Source maps are generated at build time and consumed by DevTools.
- A [[Module Bundler]] (Webpack, Vite, esbuild) resolves `import`/`require` into a dependency graph.
- Bundling runs on a build machine, never in the end user's browser.
- [[Minification]] strips whitespace and shortens names at build time.
- [[Tree Shaking]] drops unused exports at build time.
- [[Code Splitting]] is decided at build time.
- A code-split chunk is actually fetched at runtime, from your machine to their server, when the user reaches that route.
- [[Transpiling]] (Babel) converts newer syntax to older syntax at build time.
- No build step — bundling, minification, tree shaking, transpiling — happens in the end user's browser.

## Core analogy: The DOM as a physical stage set

The DOM is the actual, physical set built on stage — every prop and piece of furniture is a live object you can walk up to and rearrange. HTML is the script describing what the set should look like; the DOM is that script actually built out into a manipulable structure in memory, on **your machine**, inside the browser.

## DOM and Virtual DOM

| Stage concept | Term | Where it happens |
|---|---|---|
| The actual physical props and furniture on stage | DOM — a tree of node objects the browser maintains | **Your machine**, in the browser's rendering engine, queried/mutated via `document.querySelector`, `element.textContent`, etc. |
| Stagehands re-measuring and rebuilding the whole set vs. just repainting a surface | Reflow (expensive — layout recalculation) vs. repaint (cheaper — pixels only) | Both happen on **your machine**, triggered by the browser's rendering engine after a DOM mutation |
| Handing a stagehand a marked-up blueprint instead of walking on stage yourself every time | Virtual DOM ([[React]] etc.) — a lightweight JS object tree, diffed against the previous one | Entirely on **your machine**, in the JS engine, before any real DOM touch happens |
| The stagehand figures out the minimum real changes needed and only touches the real stage for those | Reconciliation/diffing, batching updates | **Your machine** — the framework's JS code, running in the same renderer process as your own code |

Hands-on DOM work from the course: [[Selecting Nodes]], [[Modifying Documents]], [[DOM Performance]], [[Event Delegation]], [[Event Propagation]].

## Debugging, conceptually

| Stage concept | Term | Where it happens |
|---|---|---|
| A stack of plates showing exactly which function called which | Call stack, viewed in DevTools "Sources" | **Your machine** — DevTools is inspecting the JS engine's own execution state |
| Pausing the scene mid-action to inspect every prop's state | Breakpoints | **Your machine** — pauses the JS engine's execution |
| The venue's own mailroom log of every letter sent and received | Network tab — every request, response, timing, status code | **Your machine's browser** is recording this, but it's showing you activity that also touched **the network and their machine** |
| A translation key for mangled shipped code | Source maps, used to make console errors point back to original files | Generated at build time on **your machine or a build server**, consumed by DevTools on **your machine** |

## Webpacking / bundling

| Stage concept | Term | Where it happens |
|---|---|---|
| Stitching dozens of separate scene files into one continuous performance | Module bundler (Webpack, Vite, esbuild) resolving `import`/`require` into a dependency graph | Runs on **a build machine** (your dev machine, or a CI server) — never in the end user's browser |
| Stripping whitespace, shortening names | Minification | Same — **build time**, not runtime, not in the browser |
| Cutting scenes that never get performed | Tree shaking — unused exports dropped | **Build time** |
| Shipping Act 1 first, loading Act 2 only when reached | Code splitting / lazy loading | Split decided at **build time**; the deferred chunk is actually fetched later, at runtime, **from your machine to their server**, when the user reaches that route |
| Translating tomorrow's dialect into one every audience member understands | Transpiling (Babel) | **Build time**, not in the end user's browser |

Related course notes on the language itself: [[Asynchronous JS]], [[Async Functions]], [[Promise]], [[Module]], [[Package]].
